reference.source: Braddom's Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation / pain medicine references
clinicalPearls: Amputation rehabilitation is a continuum spanning preoperative counselling, surgical level selection, postoperative residual limb care, prosthetic prescription and training, and long-term follow-up
The surgical level is chosen to balance healing potential against function, with more distal levels generally allowing better function and lower energy cost of walking
Early postoperative care focuses on wound healing, oedema control with compression or rigid dressings, residual limb shaping, and prevention of contracture through positioning and stretching
Preventing hip and knee flexion contractures is essential, as these can prevent successful prosthetic fitting and mobility
Distinguish and manage the different pain types that occur, including surgical wound pain, residual limb pain from causes such as neuroma, and phantom limb pain
Prosthetic prescription is individualised to the patient's level, goals, cognition, cardiovascular fitness, and skin condition, and requires ongoing socket fit review as the limb volume changes
The energy expenditure of walking rises with more proximal amputation and with bilateral or dysvascular amputations, which must be considered when setting mobility goals
Ongoing skin surveillance of the residual limb and the contralateral limb is vital, particularly in patients with diabetes or peripheral vascular disease who are at risk of further amputation
Psychological support and addressing body image, mood, and social reintegration are integral to successful rehabilitation
reference.pathophysiology: Most amputations in adults result from complications of peripheral vascular disease and diabetes, with trauma, malignancy, and infection accounting for others. After surgery the residual limb undergoes healing, oedema resolution, and progressive volume reduction and reshaping over weeks to months. Loss of the limb alters biomechanics and substantially increases the metabolic cost of locomotion, while neural changes from severed nerves and central reorganisation give rise to phantom phenomena and neuroma-related pain. Successful prosthetic use depends on a well-healed, appropriately shaped, and pain-free residual limb with adequate proximal joint mobility and strength.
additionalDifferentials: Residual limb wound infection or dehiscence
Ischaemia of the residual limb requiring revision to a higher level
Neuroma causing focal residual limb pain
Heterotopic ossification in the residual limb
additionalInvestigations: Vascular assessment to evaluate healing potential and select amputation level
Wound and skin inspection with monitoring for infection and pressure areas from the socket
Assessment of proximal joint range of motion and strength for prosthetic candidacy
Imaging of the residual limb where neuroma, bony spur, or heterotopic ossification is suspected
Cardiopulmonary and functional evaluation to inform realistic mobility goals
redFlags: Signs of residual limb infection, wound dehiscence, or systemic sepsis
Critical ischaemia of the residual or contralateral limb
New non-healing ulcer on the remaining foot in a diabetic or vascular patient
Rapidly worsening pain suggesting deep infection or ischaemia
Severe mood disturbance or suicidal ideation after limb loss
reference.prognosis: Functional outcome depends on amputation level, cause, age, comorbidity, and the state of the contralateral limb. Younger traumatic amputees often achieve high levels of prosthetic function, whereas older dysvascular patients, especially with bilateral or proximal amputations, may have limited walking potential and rely more on wheelchair mobility. Diligent skin care and vascular risk management are key to preventing further amputation.
pitfalls: Allowing flexion contractures to develop through poor positioning, jeopardising prosthetic fitting
Fitting a prosthesis before the wound has healed or the limb volume has stabilised
Neglecting the contralateral limb in patients at high risk of further amputation
Failing to distinguish and treat the different sources of residual and phantom pain
Setting unrealistic mobility goals without accounting for the raised energy cost of walking
management: Control residual limb oedema and promote shaping with compression garments or rigid dressings during early healing
Prevent hip and knee flexion contractures through positioning, stretching and range-of-motion exercises to preserve prosthetic candidacy
Distinguish and treat the pain types individually, using neuropathic agents for phantom limb pain and targeted measures for neuroma-related residual limb pain
Prescribe an individualised prosthesis and provide gait training, with ongoing socket-fit review as limb volume changes
Inspect the wound and socket-bearing skin regularly for breakdown, pressure areas and infection
Optimise the underlying vascular disease and diabetes and protect the contralateral limb to prevent further tissue loss
Coordinate rehabilitation medicine, prosthetics, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and psychological support as a multidisciplinary team
